compute_signals.subproblem: Expensive, high-dimensional distributed/hyper-resolution rainfall-runoff models (hundreds-to-thousands of parameters) where each forward run is costly
compute_signals.what_compute_buys: Each likelihood evaluation dominates wall-clock; GPU/many-core parallelism across parameter sets and chains (plus GPU-accelerating the forward model, ~65x reported) collapses a days-long calibration to hours, making full MCMC feasible instead of point optimization.

compute_signals.subproblem: Large-sample, many-catchment Bayesian calibration (e.g. CAMELS's 671 independent catchments)
compute_signals.what_compute_buys: Catchments are independent, so embarrassingly-parallel GPU/cloud throughput directly scales how many catchments receive proper posterior sampling rather than cheap point calibration or skipped uncertainty analysis.

compute_signals.subproblem: Multimodal posterior exploration via ensemble MCMC (DREAM/DE-MC) and SMC particle filters
compute_signals.what_compute_buys: Running thousands of chains/particles concurrently improves coverage of multimodal equifinal parameter spaces and enables cross-chain convergence diagnostics, raising effective samples per wall-clock second — though it does not reduce a single chain's integrated autocorrelation time.

items.title: Single-chain MCMC mixing: the sequential autocorrelation bottleneck
items.summary: A single Markov chain for a lumped conceptual model must run many serial iterations because posterior samples are autocorrelated; each step conditions on the previous state, and more parallel compute cannot shorten the chain's integrated autocorrelation time, only how fast samples accumulate.
items.root_link: Bears on the "what actually limits Bayesian calibration" half of the question — the single chain's autocorrelation is why lumped-model calibration is not compute-bound.
items.compute_open: none — more parallel compute buys samples-per-second but not a shorter autocorrelation time for a single chain, because τ (equivalently ESS = N/(1+2Σρ_k)) is set by target geometry and sampler, not by hardware (https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_31/reference-manual/effective-sample-size.html).
items.sequential: One converged posterior waits on one chain whose every step is a proposal from the current state plus a Metropolis accept/reject, and a single GR4J forward run is only a few thousand arithmetic steps per multi-decade daily record (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022169403002257), yet the chain must run on the order of up to 10^6 generations (DREAM(D)'s default maximum T_max; https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-15-3701-2011) to overcome autocorrelation, and the answer needs only a few independent chains (DREAM(ZS) uses N = 3–5; https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608) for Gelman–Rubin checks, each keeping a tiny fraction of one GPU busy. These steps must run in order because each state conditions on the previous one, so the only way to run them at the same time is to run many independent chains in parallel, which pays off when the target is multimodal and chains are cheap (it buys coverage, not lower τ) — the nearest source that tried it is DREAM (https://research.wur.nl/en/publications/accelerating-markov-chain-monte-carlo-simulation-by-differential-).

items.title: Ensemble / differential-evolution MCMC: running many chains in parallel
items.summary: DREAM-style samplers run N chains simultaneously, generating each chain's proposal from differences of other chains' states; this improves exploration of multimodal/correlated hydrologic posteriors and enables Gelman–Rubin cross-chain diagnostics, and it is the one place where more GPUs change what gets sampled (by raising chain count) without lowering per-chain autocorrelation.
items.root_link: Bears on the "whether a shit ton of GPUs fixes it" half — GPUs buy more parallel chains (throughput and multimodal coverage), a real but bounded fix.
items.compute_open: More parallel compute buys simultaneous chains (ensemble members); standard DREAM runs N = d/2 to d (up to 2d) chains (https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608), DREAM(ZS) needs only N = 3–5, and the largest reported run uses N = 25 chains on a 25-dimensional trimodal target (https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/1553085/134391_wrcr13130_sup_0002_t02.txt), but it is still unknown whether chains beyond N = 25 further improve posterior coverage or mixing on higher-dimensional, more multimodal hydrology targets.
items.sequential: none — after burn-in the N chains' joint density factorizes and they are independent, so the ensemble already splits into N chains run simultaneously (https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608).

items.title: Expensive distributed / high-dimensional forward models (MT-DREAM(ZS), MGB, SWAT)
items.summary: For spatially distributed models with hundreds-to-thousands of parameters the forward-model cost dominates the calibration budget, and the workload decomposes into thousands of independent model runs that are embarrassingly parallel across chains and parameter sets; here compute is a genuinely binding constraint that parallelism relieves.
items.root_link: Bears on the "what actually limits Bayesian calibration" half — for expensive distributed models the forward-model cost, not mixing, is the binding limit.
items.compute_open: settled: more parallel compute is already known to bind and pay off here — the forward model dominates the budget (DREAM needed about 50 million surrogate-model evaluations to converge on a 241-parameter groundwater model, https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608), distributed MT-DREAM(ZS) reports "spectacular performance improvement" on that same 241-parameter problem (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2011wr010608), and GPU optimization of the MGB model yields up to 20× CPU speedup for calibration and 24× (CPU) / 65× (GPU) for simulations (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envsoft.2021.105271).
items.sequential: none — the calibration already decomposes into independent forward-model runs evaluated in parallel across chains and multiple simultaneous proposals, so it is embarrassingly parallel (https://doi.org/10.1029/2011WR010608).

items.title: Large-sample multi-catchment calibration (CAMELS)
items.summary: Calibrating many catchments (CAMELS provides 671 US catchments) is embarrassingly parallel because each catchment is independently calibratable, so GPU/cloud throughput directly determines how many catchments get a proper Bayesian treatment rather than point optimization.
items.root_link: Bears on the "whether a shit ton of GPUs fixes it" half — at CAMELS scale, throughput determines how many catchments can be afforded full Bayesian treatment.
items.compute_open: More parallel compute buys catchments given full Bayesian treatment instead of point optimization; the largest published set is CAMELS's 671 US catchments (https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html), and it is still unknown what extending full Bayesian treatment to all catchments above 671 (or globally) would change about large-sample hydrological conclusions.
items.sequential: none — the catchments are independently calibratable, so the study already splits into one independent calibration per catchment (https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/21/5293/2017/hess-21-5293-2017.html).

items.id: SAE feature extraction on learned rainfall-runoff models
items.title: Train sparse autoencoders on LSTM rainfall-runoff internals to expose representation-level equifinality
items.summary: Apply Goodfire-style sparse autoencoders to LSTM cell-state activations to recover a sparse dictionary of hydrological features, then ask which features are uniquely constrained by the runoff record and which interchangeable feature sets reproduce it, reframing the framer's equifinality as non-identifiability of internal features.
items.root_link: Bears on framer.md's equifinality claim (Beven & Binley: many parameter sets reproduce the hydrograph equally well) by asking the same question at the level of a learned model's internal features.
items.compute_open: More parallel compute buys layers and features analysed: SAE dictionaries reach millions of features on single layers of models up to Llama-3.3-70B (https://www.goodfire.com/blog/a-practical-guide-to-saes), while the only geoscience application stops at simplified MLPs and one precipitation classifier (https://doi.org/10.1029/2025jh000769); what is unknown above that is whether SAE features trained on deep LSTM cell states across the 531 CAMELS catchments stay monosemantic and hydrological rather than fragmenting.
items.sequential: The chain is train LSTM -> dump cell-state activations -> train SAE -> autointerp labels -> correlate features with hydrological states (~5 serial steps); one answer needs one LSTM plus one SAE per layer, each well under a single GPU (an LSTM over 531 basins is single-GPU-scale, https://hess.copernicus.org/articles/23/5089/2019/). Only the within-layer chain must run in order (SAE training waits on that layer's activations), but SAEs for different layers are mutually independent and would run concurrently on separate GPUs if each per-layer SAE were the dominant cost, which is how Goodfire trained independent single-layer SAEs (layer 19 of the 8B model, layer 50 of the 70B model, https://www.goodfire.com/blog/sae-open-source-announcement), though no source has done this for LSTM hydrology models.

items.id: Feature steering to map the identifiable manifold
items.title: Steer SAE features of a differentiable rainfall-runoff model to separate identifiable from equifinal directions
items.summary: Use Goodfire-style feature steering on a differentiable RR model (LSTM or autodiff GR4J) to measure which features causally change the simulated runoff and which do not, producing an intervention-based map of the posterior geometry that sets the autocorrelation time.
items.root_link: Bears on framer.md's core claim that the autocorrelation time and equifinality are properties of posterior geometry, by causally mapping which parameter/feature directions actually move the simulated hydrograph.
items.compute_open: More parallel compute buys features analysed: steering is published only for individual features or small top-k sets per output (https://www.goodfire.com/research/understanding-and-steering-llama-3), even though SAE dictionaries reach millions of features (https://www.goodfire.com/blog/a-practical-guide-to-saes); what is unknown above that is whether exhaustively steering a full dictionary recovers the complete identifiable-versus-equifinal direction set or whether sparse causal coverage already suffices.
items.sequential: The chain is train differentiable RR model -> train SAE -> gradient attribution ranks features -> steer each feature and re-run the forward model to score the likelihood change -> assemble the identifiable manifold (~5 serial steps); the answer needs one forward run per (feature, steering-strength) pair, thousands of tiny runs that together barely load one GPU. Attribution must precede steering, but the per-feature steering measurements are fully independent and could be batched/vectorized across the dictionary, paying off only if the dictionary is large enough that the batch saturates the GPU; the nearest source that batched controlled interventions is SAE-V (https://arxiv.org/html/2502.06755v1).

items.title: Reparameterize the calibration with active subspaces to shorten the MCMC chain
items.summary: Identify the few data-informed directions along which the forward model varies (the active subspace) and run MCMC only on those while sampling the prior elsewhere, the non-neural, interpretability-flavored cousin of feature extraction that directly attacks the autocorrelation time through reparameterization rather than hardware.
items.root_link: Bears on framer.md's conclusion that the real lever on long chains is reparameterization or better samplers rather than more cores, by supplying exactly such a reparameterization.
items.compute_open: More parallel compute buys gradient samples used to estimate the active subspace: published demonstrations stop at M=300 gradient samples recovering a dominant one-dimensional subspace (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1506.04190) and at a 100-dimensional forward model with a two-dimensional active subspace (https://doi.org/10.1137/15m1042127); what is unknown above that is whether a single linear subspace still captures RR posteriors carrying the artificial multimodality from cheap integrators (https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1029/2009WR008648).
items.sequential: The chain is draw M gradient samples (two forward evaluations each by finite difference, or one adjoint pass) -> average the outer products into the active-subspace matrix -> eigendecompose -> run MCMC on the active variables only (~4 serial steps); the answer needs M gradient samples plus one MCMC chain, and one GR4J forward is so cheap that a single GPU stays nearly idle. The M gradient samples are mutually independent and only the active-variable MCMC must run serially, so the samples could run in parallel if the forward model were expensive enough to justify it; the nearest source that tried this is Constantine, Kent & Bui-Thanh's active-subspace-accelerated MCMC (https://doi.org/10.1137/15m1042127).

value.option_title: Reparameterize the calibration with active subspaces to shorten the MCMC chain
value.question: Does the rainfall-runoff calibration posterior have a low-dimensional active subspace, and does running MCMC only on it shorten chains more than more GPUs do?
value.hypothesis: A few data-informed directions carry the rainfall-runoff posterior's variation, so MCMC on them mixes faster and beats parallel copies.

compute_axis.quantity: gradient samples drawn to estimate the active subspace

held_fixed: 10 inactive prior samples per reconstructed parameter draw

predictions.if_lever: More parallel gradient samples make the eigenvalue gap widen enough that the reparameterized chain's ESS beats both baselines only at high counts.
predictions.if_not: The eigenvalue gap is already clear at 300 gradient samples, so more samples leave the ESS verdict unchanged: compute is not the lever.
predictions.decision_rule: Compute is the lever only if the spectral gap (ratio of the two largest estimated eigenvalues) at 100000 samples is at least 2x that at 300, or the accelerated chain's minimum ESS at 100000 is at least 2x that at 300; otherwise compute is not the lever.
predictions.noise_rule: Each spectral estimate is repeated with 10 independent prior-sample batches (bootstrap ranges, as in the published procedure); each MCMC run uses 3 seeds, and a difference is declared only when ranges do not overlap.
predictions.expected_why: Published demos already find the dominant gap at 300-1000 samples, and the framer holds that autocorrelation is set by posterior geometry, not by sample count.

value.compute_tested_why: The plan sweeps the number of gradient samples from 100 to 100000, the quantity more parallel GPUs buy, and checks whether it changes the eigenvalue gap and the ESS verdict.
value.scored_against: A long serial Metropolis-Hastings reference chain on the same GR4J posterior (posterior mean and covariance within tolerance), plus the published two-parameter quadratic reproduction.

restructuring.sequential_part: Four serial steps: draw gradient samples, average outer products, eigendecompose, then run the active-variable Markov chain.
restructuring.method: Gradient samples are mutually independent, so they run concurrently across GPUs; only the eigendecomposition and the short low-dimensional chain remain serial.
restructuring.condition: The GR4J negative log-likelihood must show a spectral gap (few large eigenvalues) so the active variables are few and the per-step conditional average is cheap; the pilot measures this spectrum before the main spend.
restructuring.baseline_sequential: Fastest serial run: JAX-compiled random-walk Metropolis on all four GR4J parameters, proposal variance tuned to roughly 25 percent acceptance, 500000 forward evaluations.
restructuring.baseline_copies: Independent vanilla Metropolis chains started from dispersed points, one per GPU, run side by side on the same instance, timed in wall-clock per effective sample.

scope_gap: Only a four-parameter daily lumped model and CAMELS catchments; the result says nothing about expensive distributed models with hundreds of parameters or likelihoods with explicit input and structural error.

novelty.closest_prior: Constantine, Kent and Bui-Thanh's active-subspace MCMC: a 100-parameter forward model, 1000 gradient samples, 500k evaluations; minimum ESS rose 604 to 81986 versus vanilla.
novelty.left_open: Whether a single linear subspace still captures rainfall-runoff posteriors whose cheap fixed-step integrators add artificial bimodality, and above 1000 gradient samples.

limits: Only synthetic and CAMELS daily lumped models; won't prove active subspaces work for distributed, high-dimensional, or input-error-dominated calibrations.
value.test_summary: Reproduce the published active-subspace MCMC, then run it on four-parameter GR4J while sweeping gradient samples 100 to 100000, against a serial vanilla Metropolis chain and side-by-side vanilla chains, comparing eigenvalue gaps and effective sample size per evaluation.

value.question: Does GPU parallelism change how many of the 671 CAMELS catchments can get full Bayesian calibration instead of point optimization?
value.hypothesis: Each catchment calibrates independently, so GPU batching turns full Bayesian treatment of all 671 into a cheap throughput problem, not a blocker.

compute_axis.quantity: catchments given full Bayesian MCMC treatment

predictions.if_lever: One GPU gives >=20x over CPU and finishes all 671 in under an hour, so compute is the lever here.
predictions.if_not: Vectorized CPU finishes all 671 in a couple of hours, so throughput does not decide which catchments get full Bayesian treatment.
predictions.decision_rule: if_lever iff GPU wall-clock for 671 catchments < 1 hour AND the GPU beats the vectorized CPU baseline by >=20x; otherwise (including a 5-20x speedup) count as if_not.
predictions.noise_rule: Time each arm 3 times with different seeds and report median wall-clock; the speedup is deterministic so seed noise <5%; confirm batching by throughput-vs-batch-size (67/335/671).
predictions.expected_why: GR4J's forward model is so cheap that full Bayesian over 671 catchments is a small job once vectorized, so compute is not the blocker.

value.compute_tested_why: The test varies the number of catchments (67/335/671) and measures whether per-catchment wall-clock stays flat as parallel work grows, i.e. whether GPU throughput is the lever that buys full Bayesian treatment.
value.scored_against: airGR reference GR4J (calibration NSE 0.495 on its example basin) and R-hat < 1.2 convergence; GPU result compared with the vectorized CPU baseline within the 20x threshold.

items.page_quote: We present a new data set of attributes for 671 catchments in the contiguous United States (CONUS) minimally impacted by human activities.
items.note: The only checkable factual claim, the 671 CAMELS catchments, matches Addor et al. 2017 (HESS abstract), which I fetched; the rest is a plan question needing no source.

items.page_quote: We present a new data set of attributes for 671 catchments in the contiguous United States (CONUS) minimally impacted by human activities.
items.note: Plan-level reasoning about GPU batching (what the plan will do) needs no source; the checkable figure 'all 671' matches the CAMELS abstract.

items.page_quote: Time full Bayesian MCMC (4 chains x 1e5 iterations, R-hat<1.2) for 671 CAMELS catchments on one GPU...
items.note: Describes the plan's own protocol (100,000 serial steps per chain, four chains/catchment), not an external factual claim; consistent with the parallel-chain setup in Laloy & Vrugt 2012, which notes convergence is declared at R<=1.2 ('If R<=1.2 for all j, stop'). No page source required for plan design.

items.page_quote: This method, entitled differential evolution adaptive Metropolis (DREAM), runs multiple different Markov chains in parallel and uses a discrete proposal distribution to evolve the sampler to the posterior distribution.
items.note: Plan design (independent chains run side by side); no external factual claim to check. Corresponding batching arithmetic (671x4=2,684) is consistent.

items.page_quote: Significant speedups of up to 20 × (CPU) were achieved for calibration, while the scalability analysis indicated 24 × (CPU) and 65 × (GPU) for simulations with larger problem sizes.
items.note: The >=20x value matches Freitas et al. 2022 ('up to 20 × (CPU) ... for calibration'; 65x GPU for larger simulations); the under-an-hour finish is the plan's own prediction and needs no source.

items.page_quote: Vectorized CPU finishes all 671 in a couple of hours, so throughput does not decide which catchments get full Bayesian treatment.
items.note: Plan-level design predication about its own CPU baseline; contains no external factual claim to check against a page.

items.page_quote: Convergence is declared when R<=1.2 for all j...
items.note: Describes what the plan will measure (design, no source needed) using figures previously checked: 671 catchments (CAMELS abstract) and the plan's own 4-chain/1e5-iteration protocol.

items.page_quote: This work aims at performance optimizations on the MGB ('Modelo de Grandes Bacias') hydrological model and the MOCOM-UA (Multi-Objective Complex Evolution) calibration method for two watersheds. Significant speedups of up to 20 × (CPU) were achieved for calibration, while the scalability analysis indicated 24 × (CPU) and 65 × (GPU) for simulations with larger problem sizes.
items.note: Freitas et al. 2022 page confirms the 20x CPU calibration speedup and that the work is GPU optimization of a single distributed hydrological model (MGB), not batched MCMC across many GR4J catchments. Year 2022 (Feb) matches 'Freitas et al. 2022'.

items.page_quote: The optimizations target state-of-the-art CPU/GPU systems, exploiting techniques that include AVX-512 vectorization, and multi-core (CPU) and many-core (GPU) parallelisms. Significant speedups of up to 20 × (CPU) were achieved for calibration...
items.note: The s_mgb page describes distributed-model calibration optimization only; nothing on it reports batched GPU MCMC giving 671 CAMELS catchments full Bayesian GR4J treatment, consistent with the gap claim.

items.page_quote: The parameter set corresponding to the best criterion is the following: X1 165.05, X2 6.46, X3 422.50, X4 2.45. The Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency criterion computed on the calibration period is better (0.495) than with the generalist parameter sets...
items.note: airGR page shows exactly parameter set X=(165.05, 6.46, 422.50, 2.45) and calibration NSE 0.495 for its example basin.

items.page_quote: This study also involves assessments of the limitations of the source data sets used to compute catchment attributes, as well as detailed descriptions of how the attributes were computed.
items.note: Scope/limit statements of the plan itself (GR4J only, US CAMELS unless global stretch, no single-chain mixing claims); no external factual claim to check.
